title: Pennsylvania: an opening for persecuted believers

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Pennsylvania offered Mennonites and other persecuted communities a place to worship and establish new homes.
paragraphs: William Penn’s new settlement offered an opening for European believers who had faced restrictions and persecution. The exhibit associates Penn and George Fox, the Quaker founder, with invitations to religious minorities in 1681–1682. Mennonites were among those encouraged to settle in “Penn’s Woods,” where freedom of worship and a charter of liberties were promised.

The invitation became a lived migration in 1683. Thirteen Mennonite-Quaker families from Krefeld crossed the Atlantic aboard the Concord and reached Philadelphia on 6 October after a ten-week voyage. They established homes in the Germantown area. This movement joined the search for freedom of conscience to the practical work of building a congregation, earning a living, and helping fellow settlers.

title: William Rittenhouse: ministry and papermaking

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: William Rittenhouse joined Mennonite pastoral service to the trade of papermaking in early Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: William Rittenhouse was born in Germany in 1644 and learned papermaking after becoming a citizen of Amsterdam. His family crossed to New York during the 1680s and later moved to Germantown. In 1690 he helped establish the first paper mill in the American colonies, carrying a European craft into the community’s new home.

He also became the first Mennonite preacher in America. The exhibit cautiously places his selection possibly as early as 1690; that qualification is retained rather than turning an uncertain appointment into a precise date. His story links daily work, migration, and care for a gathered church. He died in 1708, the year Germantown Mennonites built their first log meetinghouse.

title: Swiss believers condemned to the galleys

date.label: Mid-seventeenth century
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: The end of some executions did not end the coercion of Anabaptist believers; forced labor and exile continued.
paragraphs: The exhibit’s account of the mid-seventeenth century describes Anabaptists condemned to row galley ships in the Mediterranean and other coastal waters. Forced labor separated believers from their homes and congregations and exposed them to grueling punishment. A change in the form of punishment did not mean that liberty of conscience had been granted.

This history belongs beside the later accounts of confiscation, secret meetings, and expulsion from Bern. Together they explain why the movement’s story includes both steadfast worship under pressure and migration in search of refuge. The panel gives no individual prisoners’ names for this episode; specific lives should be added from identified prison, church, or Martyrs’ Mirror accounts rather than assigned to unnamed figures in the painting.

title: Anabaptist hunters and the expulsion from Bern

date.label: 1700–1743; expulsion in 1711
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Bounties, confiscation, hidden worship, and forced migration shaped the lives of Swiss Anabaptists in the early eighteenth century.
paragraphs: Bern authorized armed hunters to find Anabaptist believers, especially preachers. A bounty rewarded captures; property could then be confiscated and the prisoner expelled. The exhibit dates this organized pursuit to 1700–1743. Believers sought hidden places for worship, including mountain caves, rather than surrendering the convictions that had brought them into conflict with the authorities.

In 1711 the canton chartered boats to carry Anabaptists north on the Rhine. The exhibit records four boats carrying about four hundred people to the Netherlands. The recently divided Amish and Swiss Brethren sometimes resisted traveling on the same boats, showing that outward persecution did not erase painful disagreements within the brotherhood.

Many of the Swiss Brethren or Mennonites subsequently returned toward the Palatinate, while Amish refugees settled in Dutch territory. The route from Bern through the Rhine and the Netherlands therefore represents both enforced removal and the rebuilding of congregational life. The exhibit records the discontinuation of the special police force in 1743.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9364, caption E, I

title: The Amish division and the call for renewal

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Disagreement over communion, church discipline, and relations with sympathetic outsiders divided the Swiss Brethren.
paragraphs: By the 1690s some Swiss Brethren in Switzerland and the Alsace–South Rhine region believed that accommodations with the state church had weakened the brotherhood’s witness. Jakob Ammann spoke for leaders who sought renewed faithfulness. The dispute concerned the frequency of communion, social avoidance of those who had left the church, and relations with people in the state church who sympathized with the Anabaptists but would not join them.

The exhibit names Hans Reist as an elder challenged by Ammann. The disputed outsiders were called the “True-Hearted.” The question was practical as well as doctrinal: how should a disciplined community of disciples recognize fellowship, show charity, and maintain the boundaries of church membership?

Several contentious meetings failed to restore agreement, and the two groups separated. The panel dates this phase of renewal and division to 1693–1694. Later Amish congregations carried the resulting church order into new regions, but their later migrations and divisions should be followed as further chapters rather than compressed into this first dispute.

title: A meetinghouse at Germantown

date.label: 1708; stone replacement in 1770
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: A log meetinghouse gave the Germantown Mennonites a settled place for congregational worship.
paragraphs: The first Mennonite meetinghouse at Germantown was a log structure erected in 1708. The congregation grew in a settlement shaped by migration from Krefeld and other European communities. A permanent place of assembly supported the shared worship and church life that believers had sought freedom to practice in Pennsylvania.

In 1770 the log structure was replaced by a stone building. The exhibit follows its use into the twentieth century and remembers the congregation’s continuing life. The two dates mark distinct stages: 1708 is the beginning of the meetinghouse, while 1770 belongs to the surviving stone structure. They are not competing dates for the same building.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9364, caption G

title: Alexander Mack and the gathered Brethren

date.label: Documented activity 1708–1729
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Alexander Mack helped gather believers at Schwarzenau for baptism and a shared life ordered by the New Testament.
paragraphs: Alexander Mack grew up in the Reformed Church in the Palatinate and was influenced by Pietism and Anabaptism. With other believers at Schwarzenau, he came to regard personal confession of faith as necessary to baptism. In August 1708 five men and three women met at the Eder River. One member baptized Mack, who then baptized the other seven.

The Church of the Brethren’s account connects this beginning to peaceful action, plain and compassionate living, and the common search for obedience to Christ. Evangelists carried their message into other parts of Germany, Switzerland, and the Netherlands. The movement called its members brethren and sought to give their profession of faith visible expression in community.

Persecution and economic hardship later contributed to migration. Peter Becker led a group to North America in 1719; the Germantown congregation was organized in 1723, and Mack brought a further group in 1729. These related Brethren beginnings are part of the supplied timeline’s account of renewal and migration.

Church of the Brethren: institutional history

title: Johannes Nafziger and the care of Amish congregations

date.label: Born c. 1706; ministry documented 1765–1770
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Johannes Nafziger supported Amish congregations through personal assistance and written guidance for ministry.
paragraphs: Johannes Nafziger, born about 1706, served as an elder of the Amish congregation at Essingen in the Palatinate. Between 1765 and 1770 he helped Amish congregations in the Netherlands. His work belonged to a church life spread across borders after persecution and migration had dispersed the Swiss Anabaptist family.

At the congregations’ request, Nafziger wrote an extended letter explaining baptism, marriage, and the ordination of preachers. The letter became a form of ministers’ manual for Amish communities in South Germany. This surviving description shows how written counsel helped congregations preserve a shared order of worship and pastoral care when distance made regular personal contact difficult. The exhibit does not supply his death date.

title: Krefeld: refuge, work, and Mennonite community

date.label: Seventeenth and eighteenth centuries
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Mennonites at Krefeld established a community whose weaving and trade brought a measure of protection.
paragraphs: Mennonites settled at Krefeld early in the seventeenth century and developed linen and silk weaving. Their trade extended beyond the city. The exhibit links their prosperity to protection and favorable taxation under Prussian rulers. Krefeld also became a point of departure for families who sailed on the Concord to Pennsylvania in 1683.

The relationship between economic usefulness and religious protection is visible in the royal visits remembered by the city. Krefeld’s municipal history identifies the visitor in 1751 as Friedrich II, Frederick the Great, and describes his contacts with the von der Leyen silk manufacturers. The exhibit’s wording “Friedrich Wilhelm II” is not repeated here as a verified identification; the municipal account supplies the corrected name.

Krefeld’s place in this history is therefore both a refuge and a migration junction. Some believers built enduring congregational and commercial lives there, while others carried their faith and skills across the Atlantic.

title: Jacob Hochstetler and the test of nonresistance

date.label: September 1757
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: The Hochstetler family’s ordeal at Northkill became a remembered test of refusing violence in the face of danger.
paragraphs: In September 1757, during the French and Indian War, the Jacob Hochstetler family awoke to an attack at their cabin at Northkill in northern Berks County, Pennsylvania. The sons wanted to defend the household with guns. The exhibit recounts that Jacob reminded them of Christ’s teaching and would not permit violent self-defense.

Three family members were killed; Jacob and two sons were taken prisoner. The account is remembered because nonresistance was tested at the point of immediate danger and terrible personal loss. The panel does not name the other family members or give a full account of their captivity, so those details remain outside this summary rather than being filled in from the painting.

title: Worship behind the street front in Holland

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Dutch Mennonites worshiped in meeting places whose outward appearance was restricted even as congregational life continued within.
paragraphs: The exhibit describes Dutch Mennonite meeting places in the eighteenth century as hidden behind the façades of commercial buildings. Permission to gather did not necessarily include permission to make the congregation publicly conspicuous. The street frontage therefore concealed spaces in which believers could assemble for worship.

Inside, the meeting places could be well furnished, and the panel records the use of organs in many congregations after the middle of the century. This episode provides a concrete view of changing Dutch church life: the limits imposed by public authorities, the arrangements made to continue worship, and developments in congregational practice over time. It belongs alongside the separate Waterlander, Flemish, Frisian, Lamb, and Sun histories on the branch chart.

title: From Prussia to Chortitza and Molotschna

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Scouts, wagon journeys, and new villages linked Prussian Mennonites to settlements in the Russian Empire.
paragraphs: Invitations to settle in the southern Russian Empire drew the attention of Prussian Mennonites seeking religious freedom. In 1786 they sent Jacob Hoeppner and Johann Bartsch to examine the proposed region. The exhibit connects the invitation with Catherine the Great and records the scouts’ journey as a distinct step before family migration.

In 1788 an initial party of fifty set out by wagon and was joined by others, forming a company of 228 families. After a winter encampment, they resumed the journey early in 1789 by sleigh and wagon. The Chortitza settlement developed into fifteen villages with about four hundred families by 1800, according to the panel.

A second major movement brought 365 families to Molotschna between 1804 and 1806, about one hundred miles south of Chortitza. The supplied timeline’s different colony and fellowship lines grow out of these settlements. Migration carried church life, farming, family ties, and the search for an ordered Christian community into a new setting.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9364, caption N, Q

title: Hutterite communities under coercion in 1761

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Arrest and compulsory religious instruction disrupted Hutterite communal life in Austria and Hungary.
paragraphs: The exhibit marks 1761 as a severe crisis for Hutterite communities in Austria and Hungary. It recounts arrests involving Jesuit authorities, compulsory attendance at Catholic services, and the detention of leaders in monasteries for instruction. The community remembered by the panel had been reduced to only a few dozen survivors.

Communal living was also abandoned under this pressure. The panel connects this loss to its later restoration in Russian settlements. The episode helps explain why the Hutterite timeline is a sequence of refuge, disruption, renewed shared life, and further migration rather than a stationary institution. Its witness remained bound to the conviction that disciples should share their life and possessions.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9364, caption O

title: The River Brethren and believers’ baptism

date.label: 1778; Brethren in Christ name by 1863
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: A revival among Pennsylvania Mennonite communities contributed to the gathering of the River Brethren.
paragraphs: The exhibit places the beginnings of the River Brethren within a revival that affected Mennonite communities in America. In 1778 John Engel and a friend identified only as Whitmer baptized one another in a river. Their act joined a profession of renewed faith to an outward baptism and the formation of a gathered church.

The community became known as the River Brethren and, by 1863, adopted the name Brethren in Christ. The broader tradition page follows its Anabaptist, Pietist, and later evangelical relationships. The panel does not supply Whitmer’s given name, and the name is retained as recorded rather than expanded without evidence.

title: Ephrata and the German Martyrs’ Mirror

date.label: 1748 edition; Revolutionary-era episode labeled 1776
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: The Ephrata printing of Martyrs’ Mirror carried the memory of faithful witnesses to German-speaking readers in Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: Translation and printing at Ephrata gave German-speaking readers access to Martyrs’ Mirror. The Mennonite archival catalogue preserves descriptions of the title page, pages, and binding of the Ephrata edition dated 1748. That publication belongs to the transmission of the martyrs’ letters, testimonies, and examples across language and ocean.

The exhibit labels its Ephrata scene 1776 and then recounts a Revolutionary-era raid for paper, including copies of Martyrs’ Mirror, to make gun wadding. Its date is therefore kept separate from the book’s earlier printing date. In the panel’s account, a book preserving the witness of Christians who refused violence was drawn into the material demands of war.

The story connects the preservation of testimony to the practical history of translation, paper, printing, and reading. Ephrata is included here for that direct connection with Martyrs’ Mirror, while the complete source collection remains available for reading the accounts themselves.

title: Mennonite migration into Canada

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Revolution, conscience, and the search for farmland contributed to Mennonite and Amish settlement in Canada.
paragraphs: The American Revolution raised difficult questions of allegiance and conscience for some Mennonites. The exhibit follows settlers who moved into Canada after the war, first toward Nova Scotia and the Niagara Peninsula, and then to the Waterloo area around 1800. These movements enlarged the northern geography of congregational life.

A later Amish migration is associated with Christian Nafziger. He traveled from Germany to America in 1821, reached Waterloo in 1822, and explored the procedures for establishing a settlement. Returning to Germany, he recruited families who arrived in Canada in 1826 and began building homes and clearing land. The two movements share a Canadian destination but arose at different times and should not be collapsed into one arrival.

title: Jonas Stutzman and the first Amish settlement at Walnut Creek

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Jonas Stutzman’s life joined pioneer settlement, teaching, and an intensely personal expectation of Christ’s return.
paragraphs: Jonas Stutzman came to the Walnut Creek Valley in 1809 and is remembered by the exhibit as the first white settler of eastern Holmes County. He operated an early sawmill and taught school for a number of years. His work belonged to the practical beginnings of an Amish community that needed homes, timber, and education as well as congregational life.

In the late 1840s Stutzman studied premillennial teaching and wrote three pamphlets calling readers to repentance in expectation of Christ’s imminent return. He settled on June 1853 as the expected time. He also began dressing in white and made a special wooden chair associated with his expectation of Christ’s reign. These were Stutzman’s recorded convictions and actions, not a date the site presents as fulfilled prophecy or a belief assigned to all Amish people.

His long life, from 1787 to 1871, spans the opening of the Ohio settlements and their development into established communities. The panel preserves both the contribution of a pioneer and the distinctive religious expectations for which he was remembered.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption A

title: Christian Nafziger and the journey to Ontario

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Christian Nafziger explored a Canadian settlement and recruited Amish Mennonite families to establish homes there.
paragraphs: Christian Nafziger left his family in Germany and traveled to America in 1821, entering through New Orleans. He then made his way north along the Mississippi and Ohio rivers toward Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Advice that land was cheaper in Canada led him to continue his search there.

In 1822 he reached Waterloo, Ontario, and approached the government about establishing a settlement. He returned to Germany and encouraged Amish Mennonite families to join the migration. The families arrived in 1826, built homes, and cleared land. Nafziger’s journey shows the advance work behind a migration: scouting, negotiation, return travel, and the gathering of people willing to begin again.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption B

title: Westward settlement from Pennsylvania to Ohio, Indiana, and Iowa

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Amish and Mennonite families formed new settlements across the expanding American Midwest.
paragraphs: The exhibit follows Amish and Mennonite families west after the opening of the Ohio territory. It places the first settlers in the region in 1808–1809 and a further movement after 1812. Homes and congregations developed in places where forests, roads, and farms still required extensive work.

By 1841 families from Somerset County and Holmes County were moving into northern Indiana. Settlement in Illinois and Iowa developed during the same broad period: the panel notes mid-state Illinois in 1832–1850 and Kalona, Iowa, by 1846. These were distinct local beginnings, connected by kinship and church relationships rather than a single centrally directed migration.

The source’s later account of the Walnut Creek meetinghouse shows that settlement also brought questions about worship and church order. Families carried their convictions with them while deciding how their new communities should organize schooling, meeting places, and relationships with neighboring congregations.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption C, G

title: Samuel Frölich and the Apostolic Christian beginnings

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Samuel Frölich’s preaching gathered believers from Reformed and Mennonite backgrounds into a new church community.
paragraphs: Samuel Frölich entered ministry in the Reformed Church in Switzerland in 1828 but was later excluded from the state church. At Langnau he gathered a congregation that drew members from both Reformed and Mennonite backgrounds. The exhibit connects this movement with the Apostolic Christian Church.

Its American beginnings are dated in the panel to 1852 among Amish Mennonites in New York. Later settlements developed in Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. Frölich died in Strasbourg in 1857. His story is included because the supplied source explicitly follows the movement’s relationship with Amish and Mennonite people; it does not make all of those older communities part of the new church.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption D

title: John Holdeman and a call to renewal

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: John Holdeman gathered a separate fellowship after a religious awakening and a call to preach in Ohio.
paragraphs: John Holdeman’s concern for the spiritual life of the church followed a deep religious experience at his home in Wayne County, Ohio. He believed he was called to preach, but the existing church did not affirm that ministry. In 1859 he and others began worshiping separately, and their fellowship developed as the Church of God in Christ, Mennonite.

Holdeman subsequently moved with followers to Missouri and then to Kansas. The exhibit notes the growth of the movement and the arrival of converts from the Kleine Gemeinde in Manitoba. Renewal, preaching, migration, and congregational discipline were therefore closely connected in its development.

The church’s own account places believers’ baptism, conversion, nonresistance, and an ordered Christian life at the heart of its witness. Holdeman’s biography provides the human thread behind the branch and event entries rather than leaving the new fellowship as an unexplained line on a chart.

title: Mennonite mission from the Netherlands to Java

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: A Dutch mission association helped begin a Mennonite mission in Java with support across national boundaries.
paragraphs: The Dutch Mennonite Mission Association was founded in 1847 to carry the gospel into the Dutch colonies. The exhibit records support from Mennonite congregations in Germany and Russia and from some communities in the United States. The work connected geographically separated churches through giving, personnel, and a shared desire to make the gospel known.

The first mission field opened in Java in 1851. Dutch workers were joined by German, Swiss, and Russian Mennonites. The panel connects this beginning with the later Indonesian Mennonite Church. Its reported congregation total belongs to the date of the exhibit, so it is not presented as a current count. The enduring historical point is the growth of an Indonesian church from a mission that crossed several European and North American networks.

title: Walnut Creek: meetinghouse and Amish Mennonite change

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: The first Amish meetinghouse in Holmes County became part of wider debate about congregational change.
paragraphs: The exhibit dates the first meetinghouse among the Amish of Holmes County to 1862 and identifies it with the later Walnut Creek Mennonite Church. A purpose-built meeting place was more than a construction project in communities accustomed to gathering in homes. It brought questions about inherited practice and proposed change into the life of the congregation.

A division grew between those who wished to retain older ways and those willing to accept meetinghouses and other innovations. The latter eventually joined the Mennonite Church and discontinued the Amish designation. This local account helps explain the later Amish and Amish Mennonite branches without treating every difference as the same dispute or assigning one decision to all congregations.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption G

title: Mennonite care for the wounded during the Crimean War

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Mennonites near the Crimean War cared for wounded people while declining active military service.
paragraphs: The Crimean War took place within about 160 miles of the Chortitza and Molotschna colonies, according to the exhibit. The war’s demands reached Mennonite settlements even though the fighting was not centered in their villages. Residents of the empire were called on to assist the war effort.

The panel distinguishes Mennonite refusal of active military duty from their willingness to care for wounded people in hospitals and homes. This practical service makes nonresistance visible as both a refusal to take up arms and a readiness to help the suffering. The entry concerns that response of the communities; a general military history of the war falls outside its purpose.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption H

title: Bernhard Warkentin, Philip Wiebe, and the land scouts

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Two scouts investigated North American farmland before the major migration from the Russian Empire.
paragraphs: As Mennonites in the Russian Empire became concerned about threats to their privileges, they looked west for possible new homes. In 1872 Bernhard Warkentin and Philip Wiebe traveled to North America to examine land. The exhibit names Kansas, Texas, Minnesota, the Dakota region, and Manitoba among the places they investigated.

They sent letters back to Russia describing their findings. This correspondence helped families consider migration before committing to an ocean crossing and a new settlement. The scouts’ work connects the later mass movement to identifiable people, routes, and practical decisions rather than depicting migration as an unexplained arrow between continents.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption J

title: The Budget: letters between scattered communities

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: A newspaper founded in Sugarcreek helped Amish and Mennonite communities remain in contact through local letters.
paragraphs: Samuel H. Miller founded The Budget as a weekly newspaper at Sugarcreek, Ohio, in 1890. Its distinctive contribution was the publication of letters describing life in scattered communities. Readers could learn of happenings among fellow believers beyond the reach of their own congregation or settlement.

The exhibit remembers its growth into a national publication for Amish and Mennonite readers. Its place in this history is therefore the maintenance of relationships across distance: families and congregations that migrated apart could still share news of ordinary work and community life. The founding date is the historical milestone recorded here; no current circulation figure is supplied by the panel.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption K

title: General Conference mission among Native American communities

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: General Conference Mennonites began mission work among several Native American peoples in the American West.
paragraphs: The exhibit records that the Foreign Mission Board of the General Conference Mennonite Church began this work during the 1880s. It names Arapaho, Hopi, and Cheyenne communities and identifies Oklahoma, Arizona, and Montana as locations reached by the mission.

These names locate the episode more precisely than a general statement that Mennonites spread west. They also identify the peoples among whom missionaries worked. The short panel does not supply individual missionaries’ names, the experiences of Native believers, or a detailed account of each mission. Those distinct local histories require their own records and should not be invented from the shared heading.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption L

title: Mennonite and Hutterite migration to North America

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Military-service changes and the search for secure community life contributed to migration from the Russian Empire.
paragraphs: The exhibit connects the major migration beginning in 1874 with the introduction of universal military service and wider concerns about Mennonite and Hutterite life in the Russian Empire. About eighteen thousand people are included in its account of the movement. Families considered where they could preserve faith, nonresistance, schools, language, and community life.

Railway development made land available and encouraged settlement on the North American prairies. The Santa Fe Railroad had reached Newton, Kansas, in 1871, and its agents promoted land to immigrants. The panel places about ten thousand Mennonite settlers in the American Midwest, with others going to additional prairie states and Canadian provinces.

The migrants brought agricultural knowledge and hard winter wheat that contributed to the region’s farming. Mennonite and Hutterite communities shared parts of this migration, while their church organization and communal practices remained distinct. The related branch entries follow the Old Colony, Bergthal, Kleine Gemeinde, Mennonite Brethren, and Hutterite histories beyond arrival.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption M

title: Abraham and Miriam Friesen: mission to India

date.label: Mission began in 1890
date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Abraham and Miriam Friesen were sent from the Mennonite Brethren in Russia to begin mission work in India.
paragraphs: Abraham and Miriam Friesen are named in the exhibit as the first Mennonite missionaries to India, sent in 1890 by the Mennonite Brethren in Russia. Because their sending churches did not yet have an organized mission agency, they served through the American Baptist Missionary Society.

Other Mennonite mission programs from the United States sent workers in 1899–1900. The panel follows these beginnings toward later Mennonite and Brethren in Christ congregations in India. Its numerical totals describe the exhibit’s own period and are not reused as current statistics. The Friesens’ story records an identifiable beginning and the cooperation through which the early work became possible.

references.label: Supplied Church History exhibit, IMG_9365, caption N

title: Mennonite mission and church growth in Congo

date.basis: Date or period stated in the supplied exhibit; any additional source or qualification is identified in the references and narrative.

summary: Planning in 1911 was followed by the arrival of the first Congo Inland Mission workers in 1912.
paragraphs: Efforts to establish a Mennonite mission in Congo began in 1911. The exhibit states that the first missionaries were placed a year later by the Congo Inland Mission, subsequently known as Africa Inter-Mennonite Mission. These two dates distinguish planning from the arrival of workers.

Other work associated with the Mennonite Brethren developed alongside it. The panel points toward autonomous Mennonite churches in the Democratic Republic of Congo, extending the timeline beyond migration from Europe and North America. Its membership totals are historical exhibit figures, not a statement about present numbers. The individual African believers and congregations require further sourced accounts rather than being left as anonymous endpoints of a map.

title: Hans Hut: preaching, baptism, and imprisonment

date.label: Ministry 1526–1527; died 6 December 1527
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Hans Hut carried Anabaptist preaching across South Germany and Austria before dying in imprisonment at Augsburg.
paragraphs: Hans Hut worked as a bookbinder and traveling bookseller. Questions about infant baptism led him to examine Scripture and eventually to refuse baptism for his newborn child, at the cost of leaving his home. Hans Denck baptized him at Augsburg on 26 May 1526. He then traveled widely, preaching and baptizing in Bavaria, Franconia, Austria, and neighboring regions.

His preaching joined repentance, the suffering of disciples, and an expectation of coming judgment. He attended the 1527 gathering at Augsburg and was arrested that autumn. The exhibit dates his death to 6 December 1527, following a fire in his prison, and records the public burning of his body afterward. The historical reference preserves differing accounts of how the fire began; the outcome is clear without choosing an unsupported reconstruction.

title: Hans Denck: Scripture, conscience, and discipleship

date.label: Born c. 1500; died November 1527
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Hans Denck’s teaching and writing influenced the early Anabaptist movement in South Germany.
paragraphs: Hans Denck was educated in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew and worked in printing before becoming rector of St. Sebald School in Nuremberg. His understanding of faith brought him into conflict with the city’s clergy. In January 1525 he was banished after submitting confessions concerning his beliefs, including baptism and communion.

Denck later lived at Augsburg, where he became a leader among the Anabaptists and baptized Hans Hut in 1526. He emphasized the inward work of God and a life transformed in obedience, while relating outward baptism to a covenant with God. His brief life ended with the plague at Basel in November 1527. The supplied chart places his influence alongside other early teachers rather than giving his name to a surviving denomination.

title: Ulrich Stadler and the shared life of the brotherhood

date.label: Ministry in Moravia and Poland, 1531–1540
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Ulrich Stadler helped lead refugee communities and explained the spiritual meaning of shared possessions.
paragraphs: Ulrich Stadler came from Brixen in the Tyrol and worked as a mining official at Sterzing. After joining the Anabaptists he fled persecution to Moravia. When renewed pressure reached Moravia in 1535, he and Leonhard Lochmaier led believers to refuge in Poland, where two communities were established.

Stadler returned to Moravia with about one hundred people in 1537 and led a settlement at Bucovic. Following discussions with Hans Amon, he joined the Hutterite brotherhood. His writings describe a surrendered heart devoted to God and the brethren and connect that discipleship with the sharing of goods, care for the community, and discipline. He died in 1540, leaving a written witness to the common life practiced by these refugees.

title: Melchior Hoffman: preaching and long imprisonment

date.label: Born c. 1494/1495; imprisoned 1533; death date uncertain
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Melchior Hoffman spread Anabaptist teaching in northern Europe and spent years imprisoned in Strasbourg.
paragraphs: Melchior Hoffman was a furrier from the Schwäbisch Hall region who became an itinerant preacher during the Reformation. His work carried him through northern Europe before his association with Anabaptism. The supplied panel remembers his extensive preaching, his arrest at Strasbourg in 1533, and a confinement lasting more than ten years.

Hoffman urged repentance and expected Christ’s return, assigning prophetic significance to Strasbourg. His message influenced the early Dutch movement, while later followers took different paths. His imprisonment and writings belong to the setting in which Obbe Philips, Dirk Philips, and Menno Simons emerged. The exhibit gives approximately 1494–1544; the historical reference uses approximately 1495 and questions the precise death date. Those uncertainties remain visible rather than being converted into exact lifespan claims.

title: Peter Riedemann: a confession written in captivity

date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Peter Riedemann expressed the faith of the Hutterite brotherhood through confessions written amid persecution.
paragraphs: Peter Riedemann was an Anabaptist minister and missionary whose life included repeated imprisonment. At the age of twenty-three he wrote a confession in an Austrian castle tower; that work is now published in English as Love Is Like Fire. His writing connected faith in Christ with believers’ baptism, nonviolence, sharing, and the restoration of New Testament church life.

The Hutterite history remembers him as the author of the Rechenschaft, or Confession of Faith, among the missionaries who carried the message beyond their communities despite capture and suffering. Riedemann spent about nine years of his life in prison. He died in 1556 at a Hutterian community in Slovakia. His place on the timeline points to both the written teaching and the costly witness that sustained the brotherhood.

title: Pilgram Marpeck and the South German fellowship

date.label: Documented leadership 1525–1556
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Pilgram Marpeck joined civic experience, practical work, and written teaching in the service of Anabaptist congregations.
paragraphs: Pilgram Marpeck came from Rattenberg in the Tyrol and served in civic offices and mining administration. As mining magistrate he faced demands to hand over workers sympathetic to Anabaptist preaching. His later life and writings belonged to the South German movement, and the supplied exhibit identifies him among its leading teachers.

Marpeck helped sustain a fellowship through correspondence and theological writing. Leupold Scharnschlager became a close associate, sharing in the explanation of baptism, Christian life, and the church. Their writings show that dispersed congregations were connected by counsel and study as well as by travel. Marpeck died in 1556. The chart’s spelling “Pilgrim Marpeck” is retained as a searchable alternative to the documented name Pilgram.

title: Leupold Scharnschlager: exile and pastoral correspondence

date.label: Anabaptist ministry c. 1530–1563
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Leupold Scharnschlager cared for believers across borders after losing his home for joining the Anabaptists.
paragraphs: Leupold Scharnschlager was from the Tyrol, where he owned property near Hopfgarten. Around 1530 he joined the Anabaptists and left with his wife Anna and their daughter; his estate was confiscated in 1531. At Strasbourg he became associated with Pilgram Marpeck and extended his ministry to believers in other cities.

A letter written to Michael Leubel at Speyer in 1532 discussed baptism and original sin. The historical record also remembers expelled believers finding access to Scharnschlager’s home. These connections show pastoral care expressed through hospitality, letters, and teaching during displacement. He and Marpeck later collaborated on writings for the brotherhood. Scharnschlager died in 1563.

title: Dirk Philips and the teaching of a gathered church

date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Dirk Philips served with Menno Simons and wrote extensively about baptism, new birth, church order, and discipleship.
paragraphs: Dirk Philips was born at Leeuwarden in 1504 and was the younger brother of Obbe Philips. He joined the Anabaptist movement in the winter of 1533–1534 and later worked as an elder in the northern Netherlands, East Friesland, and northern Germany. The supplied chart also associates Dirk and Menno Simons with the organization of congregations in the Danzig–Prussian region.

His writings addressed baptism, communion, the incarnation, new birth, the ministry, marriage, and church discipline. Many were collected in the Enchiridion, or Handbook, in 1564. Philips emphasized obedience to Scripture and a visible fellowship whose members should live consistently with their confession. The application of the ban and shunning became a central concern in his work and in the disagreements among later Dutch groups. He died near Emden in 1568.

title: Obbe Philips and the early Dutch brotherhood

date.label: Born c. 1500; died 1568
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Obbe Philips helped gather the early Dutch movement before withdrawing from its ministry around 1540.
paragraphs: Obbe Philips, a barber-surgeon from Leeuwarden, became involved with Melchior Hoffman’s followers and was baptized in December 1533. He traveled among Dutch believers and took part in appointing leaders, including his brother Dirk, David Joris, and later Menno Simons. The supplied chart preserves his name as a separate early line beside the Mennonite movement.

After the crisis at Münster, Obbe’s followers became associated with a rejection of armed religious action. Obbe himself later doubted the validity of his calling and the ordinations he had performed. He withdrew from the movement around 1539–1540 and described that crisis in his later Confession. The exhibit’s “Departures” caption records this separation. His earlier work and his departure are both part of the history; the record does not turn the end of his ministry into an unnamed break on the chart.

title: High German Mennonites

date.label: Sixteenth century to the 1639 Amsterdam union
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: The High Germans connected South German and Rhineland believers with Dutch congregations and efforts toward reconciliation.
paragraphs: High German or Upper German Mennonites came originally from South Germany and the Rhine region. Some formed close ties with Swiss believers; merchants and other migrants also carried these relationships into Haarlem, Amsterdam, and Leiden. In Dutch church disputes, High German became a fellowship name associated with a less severe application of banning and shunning.

Agreements with some Frisian congregations, including the 1591 Concept of Cologne, prepared the way for later cooperation. At Amsterdam the united High German–Frisian congregation joined the Flemish congregation in 1639. The supplied chart displays this joining of lines. The name therefore describes a changing fellowship history, shaped by migration, differences over discipline, and efforts to restore peace among believers.

title: The Lamb and Sun congregations

date.label: Division in 1664; reunion in 1801
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: The Lamb and Sun names remember an Amsterdam division and the later reunion of its congregations.
paragraphs: The branch chart names the Lamb Group and Sun Group. Their names came from the emblems of their meeting places in Amsterdam. A Mennonite church marked by a lamb had been built in 1608. When the congregation divided in 1664, those who left gathered in the Zon meeting hall, whose name and sign referred to the sun.

The two congregations reunited in 1801 and used a combined lamb-and-sun identity. The chart’s joining lines therefore represent reconciliation as well as separation. These local congregational names help explain the later Dutch Mennonite association while preserving the distinct history that came before it.

title: Old Flemish Mennonites

date.label: Distinct fellowships from c. 1630
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Old Flemish congregations retained separate church relationships while other Dutch groups pursued union.
paragraphs: The chart carries an Old Flemish line beside the Lamb and Sun groups. Within that older name, Groningen and Danzig Old Flemish congregations developed distinct histories. They did not join all of the unions undertaken by other Flemish groups around 1632 and 1639. Questions of church discipline, fellowship, and congregational practice lay behind these divisions.

Groningen Old Flemish congregations emphasized plain living, a rigorous ban, and feetwashing associated with the Lord’s Supper. They also cooperated in helping Mennonites expelled from Switzerland and believers in Prussia affected by persecution or disasters. Danzig Old Flemish congregations had their own customs and connections. Keeping both histories visible prevents the exhibit’s single line from concealing the communities and practices it summarizes.

title: Joseph Stuckey and the Central Illinois Amish division

date.label: Separation in 1872; conference in 1899
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: A dispute over discipline separated Joseph Stuckey and several Illinois congregations from the wider Amish fellowship.
paragraphs: Joseph Stuckey, born in Alsace in 1825, came to America as a child and later became an Amish minister and bishop in Illinois. In 1872 a ministers’ gathering asked him to exclude a congregant who had advocated universalism. Stuckey refused to do so, although the historical account states that he did not himself hold that view. Fellowship was then withdrawn from him and his congregation.

Many Central Illinois congregations remained with Stuckey, producing the line that the exhibit calls the Stuckey Amish Schism. Their formal Central Illinois Conference was not organized until 1899. The two dates distinguish the breach in fellowship from the later conference structure and show how a local question of discipline developed into an enduring regional church history.

title: Reinländer Mennonites in Manitoba

date.label: 1875–1925 in Manitoba
date.basis: Named on the supplied branch chart; dates and biographical detail are supplied by the identified historical references.

summary: Reinländer congregations formed a distinct Old Colony church history after migration to Manitoba.
paragraphs: The exhibit lists Reinlander among its Old Colony Groups. The Reinländer Mennoniten Gemeinde was organized in Manitoba in 1875 under elder Johann Wiebe of Rosengart. Its members included immigrants from the Chortitza and Fürstenland colonies, which explains the related Alt-Kolonier or Old Colony designation.

The church also came to care for settlements in Saskatchewan. Its organization brought together elders, ministers, deacons, and congregational records in the new Canadian setting. The historical body ceased to exist in Canada after 1925 as migration and reorganization changed the community. This entry identifies the named fellowship within the broader Old Colony line instead of treating every colony-based group as interchangeable.

title: Mennonite colleges: learning within the church

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: Mennonite communities founded colleges and church schools to join academic learning with faith, congregational life, and preparation for service.
paragraphs: Mennonite education in North America grew from the needs of particular congregations and immigrant communities. The supplied timeline places Bethel College in Newton, Kansas, in 1887, associating its beginnings with Russian Mennonite immigrants who valued education. The school became one expression of a wider effort to prepare a younger generation for life in the church and in the places where Mennonites were settling.

The Elkhart Institute began in 1894 as a secondary academy. After moving to Goshen, Indiana, in 1903, it developed a collegiate curriculum and became Goshen College. In Ohio, the Middle District of the General Conference Mennonite Church established Central Mennonite College at Bluffton in 1899. The photographed account dates its change to the name Bluffton College to 1913, a chronology also reflected in the institution’s own history.

The Virginia Mennonite Conference began a church school at Harrisonburg in 1917. Known later as Eastern Mennonite University, it answered a desire for Mennonite education in the eastern United States. These schools did not all arise from the same conference or follow an identical path. Their different beginnings show congregations taking responsibility for the education and Christian formation of their own young people.

In Ontario, Mennonite leaders established Conrad Grebel College in affiliation with the University of Waterloo. Its provincial charter dates to 1961; its first classes followed in 1963. The distinction matters because the photographed timeline prints 1961, while institutional histories also commemorate the opening of teaching in 1963. Grebel’s initial purpose included religious knowledge and liberal arts for students whose university studies were in other fields, extending Mennonite educational life into a different institutional setting.

title: Berlin Bible School and preparation for service

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: A winter Bible school at Pleasant View Mennonite Church became a continuing work of Bible study and preparation for Christian service at Rosedale, Ohio.
paragraphs: In 1952, the Conservative Mennonite Conference began a winter Bible school at Pleasant View Mennonite Church near Berlin, Ohio. Its purpose was practical and spiritual: to give students an opportunity to study the Bible and prepare for Christian service. The church building served as its home for twelve years, placing the school’s beginnings within the life of a local congregation.

The school’s reach grew beyond its immediate setting. The photographed account reports that in 1963 it drew students from seventeen states and offered thirty-three courses. Those figures describe that historical moment rather than present enrollment or a current catalog. They indicate how a seasonal church-based school was becoming a shared educational work for a much wider constituency.

After the conference bought a vacant school building at Rosedale, Ohio, the Bible school moved there in 1964. The timeline follows this development into Rosedale Bible College. Read alongside the earlier Mennonite colleges, its history shows another form of church education: concentrated biblical study directed toward the work of Christian congregations and service.

title: Russian Mennonites: upheaval, relief, and new homes

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: Prosperous settlements faced revolution, hunger, and displacement, drawing Mennonite congregations into coordinated relief and renewed migration.
paragraphs: The Mennonite migrations of 1874 did not empty the communities in the Russian Empire. The photographed history describes many Mennonites remaining in the Ukrainian colonies, where some landowners and industrialists prospered between 1880 and 1917. Those settlements formed the homes, congregations, and livelihoods whose future was overturned during the revolutionary years.

Between 1917 and 1919, the movement of Red and White armies through the colony regions brought destruction, pillage, and death. The timeline connects the particular vulnerability of Mennonites with their German language and the relative wealth of some communities. This political history enters the church account through what happened to families and congregations. Famine in the aftermath made the need for food and outside help still more urgent.

Mennonite communities sent four representatives to North America to seek help. Several relief committees gathered aid, and the need to coordinate their work helped bring Mennonite Central Committee into being in 1920. Clayton Kratz was among the early workers who accompanied that response. The delegates also explored places of settlement in Canada; the photographed account describes about 20,000 Mennonites arriving between 1923 and 1930, joining communities established by an earlier migration. Relief and resettlement became connected ways for churches to bear one another’s burdens.

title: Clayton Kratz

date.label: Relief service in 1920
date.basis: The photographed account identifies Kratz’s relief service and disappearance around MCC’s beginning in 1920; it supplies no birth date or confirmed death date.

summary: Clayton Kratz was one of the early Mennonite relief workers sent to communities suffering in the aftermath of revolution in Russia.
paragraphs: Clayton Kratz entered the history of Mennonite Central Committee at its beginning. Hunger and devastation among Mennonite settlements in southern Russia had brought appeals to North American congregations. Committees gathered food and other assistance, and in 1920 they coordinated their response through the newly formed MCC. Kratz was one of the young men who went to help make that response possible.

The photographed timeline remembers three workers accompanying a shipment of food. MCC’s own historical account names those first workers as Orie Miller, Clayton Kratz, and Arthur Slagel. Their task was to help arrange the distribution of relief in a region where armies were still fighting and control of towns and settlements could change rapidly.

Kratz disappeared during this work. The panel says that he was presumably captured by the Red Army and was not heard from again; a later MCC account describes his arrest and presumed death. Neither supplies a confirmed death date in the material used here. His place in this history is therefore the documented work of relief and the loss that followed it, with the uncertainty about his final fate kept visible.

title: The Mennonite mission in Argentina

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: A mission begun in 1917 established a center at Pehuajó and became part of the growth of Mennonite congregational life in Argentina.
paragraphs: Argentina became a focus of Mennonite mission study and planning early in the twentieth century. The photographed timeline records four missionaries being appointed and sent there in 1917. It does not name them, so their individual biographies cannot be supplied from this panel alone. The dated event is the beginning of this organized work.

Two years later, in 1919, a center opened at Pehuajó, in the agricultural region west of Buenos Aires. This gave the mission a local base. The account follows the work into the life of the Iglesia Evangélica Menonita Argentina, making clear that the story concerns the formation of congregations as well as the arrival of missionaries.

The panel reports a later membership of 4,500 in forty-five congregations, without providing a separate date for that count. Those numbers belong to the photographed source and should not be read as current statistics. The enduring historical connection is the work of sharing the Christian message and gathering a church community in Argentina, one part of the wider geographical reach of Anabaptist faith.

title: The Hofer brothers and Jacob Wipf

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: Joseph, Michael, and David Hofer and their brother-in-law Jacob Wipf suffered imprisonment after refusing military participation as Hutterite conscientious objectors.
paragraphs: In 1918, four young men from Rockport Colony in South Dakota were drafted and sent to a military camp in Washington. Joseph Hofer, Michael Hofer, David Hofer, and Jacob Wipf belonged to a Hutterite community whose obedience to Christ included refusal to take part in war. Their convictions brought them into direct conflict with military demands.

The men were court-martialed and sentenced to twenty years at Alcatraz. The photographed account describes severe mistreatment during their imprisonment, including being shackled with their hands above their heads. After four months they were transferred to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Joseph and Michael died soon after their arrival in weakened condition. David was released later, while Jacob Wipf remained imprisoned until April 1919.

Hutterite remembrance places the Hofer brothers among those who suffered for faithfulness to their confession. Their story belongs beside the older accounts of costly discipleship without being confused with an account actually contained in the seventeenth-century Martyrs’ Mirror. It also helps explain the fears of the colonies around them and the movement of many Hutterite communities from the United States to Canada in 1918.

title: Hutterite communities move north

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: Wartime hostility and the costs of refusing military participation helped drive Hutterite colonies toward new homes in Canada.
paragraphs: The Hutterite move north during the First World War was a migration of communities seeking room to continue their life of faith. German speech, refusal to participate in war, and resistance to financing it made colonies targets of hostility. The photographed timeline describes open harassment of settlements in the United States during this period.

At Jamesville Colony in South Dakota, refusal to sell war bonds was followed by a raid that cost the community livestock valued in the panel at about $40,000. The imprisonment of the Hofer brothers and Jacob Wipf placed the consequences of nonresistance before other families as well. A colony’s ability to live by its convictions could no longer be taken for granted.

Many colonies prepared to leave the United States, and a substantial movement into Canada followed in 1918. Hutterite community history records settlements in Manitoba and Alberta among the different Leut. The move extended the long history of Hutterite migration in search of religious freedom, carrying communal worship, shared work, and common life into new prairie homes.

title: Jacob Siemens and the escape across the Amur

date.basis: These dates identify the escape and subsequent resettlement described by the source, not Siemens’s lifespan.

summary: Jacob Siemens led a group of more than two hundred Mennonites across the frozen Amur River into China in December 1930.
paragraphs: After the Russian Revolution, Mennonite families had settled along the Amur River in eastern Asiatic Russia. The photographed account places Jacob Siemens at the head of a party of more than two hundred people who left that region in December 1930. Their route to safety lay across the frozen river into China.

The crossing was the beginning of a longer journey. The refugees eventually reached Harbin, where they joined other groups who had fled earlier. The source gives Siemens’s name as the leader of the river crossing but provides no birth date, death date, or fuller personal biography. His profile is therefore centered on the particular act of leadership the account records.

Between 1931 and 1934, Mennonite Central Committee helped members of these refugee groups find new homes in Paraguay, Brazil, and the United States. The episode connects personal courage and group migration with the developing work of organized Mennonite relief. It belongs within the church’s history of helping displaced families rebuild their lives across national borders.

title: The Volendam and Mennonite refugees

date.basis: Years of the documented activity in the supplied timeline photographs, not necessarily a lifespan.

summary: The Volendam carried displaced Mennonites toward refuge in South America after the Second World War, with Peter and Elfrieda Dyck helping lead the transports.
paragraphs: After the Second World War, displaced Mennonite families were searching for homes in which they could begin again. The Netherlands permitted Mennonite Central Committee to charter the Volendam for a transport to Buenos Aires, followed by settlement in Paraguay. The photographed timeline dates this episode to 1947.

Two further transports followed on the same ship. The account gives a total of about 4,700 people who found refuge in South America through these voyages. That total belongs to the sequence of transports, rather than being the passenger count of a single crossing. Peter and Elfrieda Dyck helped lead several of the journeys as part of their work with refugees.

The ship’s place in Mennonite history is inseparable from the work around it: relief programs, arrangements for travel, accompaniment of families, and the search for places of settlement. The Volendam story continues the earlier history of MCC’s relief and resettlement, showing the care of displaced church communities taking a practical form after another destructive war.

title: Peter and Elfrieda Dyck

date.label: Peter: 1914–2010; Elfrieda: 1917–2004
date.basis: The range spans both lives; the individual birth and death years are stated separately in the label and biography.

summary: Peter and Elfrieda Dyck served displaced people through Mennonite Central Committee and helped lead Mennonite refugee transports to South America.
paragraphs: Peter Dyck was born in 1914 in the Am Trakt settlement in Russia and moved to Canada with his family in 1927. Elfrieda Klassen was born in 1917 in the Neu Samara settlement. In 1925 she moved with her widowed mother and siblings to Winnipeg, Manitoba. Their childhood migrations preceded the relief work for which they would later be remembered.

Under Mennonite Central Committee, Peter went to war-damaged England in 1941 to assist relief efforts. Elfrieda arrived a year later. They married in 1944 and were subsequently asked to lead a relief program in the Netherlands, assisting Mennonites fleeing Russia and later German refugees.

The Dycks accompanied several transports of displaced Mennonites aboard the Volendam to South America. In that work, the broad history of postwar migration became a responsibility toward particular families who needed food, arrangements, guidance, and a place to settle. Their names connect the story of the ship with the people who carried the work forward.

Peter later served as MCC director for Europe and North Africa, and subsequently as an administrator and communicator. Elfrieda died in 2004 and Peter in 2010. The photographed account remembers their shared refugee service as a sustained expression of Christian care, reaching from wartime relief into the rebuilding of lives after the war.

title: Merlin and Dorothy Grove

date.label: Somalia service, 1960–1962
date.basis: The date range identifies their shared mission work described here. The panel gives Merlin’s lifespan as 1929–1962 and Dorothy’s death as November 6, 2010.

summary: Merlin and Dorothy Grove served in education in Somalia; after Merlin’s killing and Dorothy’s injury, their mission colleagues offered a witness of love and forgiveness.
paragraphs: Merlin and Dorothy Grove came from Markham, Ontario, and joined the Eastern Mennonite Board of Missions for service in Somalia. Their family moved there in 1960, and Merlin began teaching. The mission’s own history identifies his work in Mogadishu and places the attack on him while he was registering students for evening classes.

On July 16, 1962, Merlin was stabbed by an attacker. Dorothy ran toward the room when she heard the disturbance and was also wounded. Merlin died, while Dorothy was taken to hospital and recovered. The source records the attack without supplying the assailant’s name; no name is added here.

At the subsequent trial, mission staff voiced love and forgiveness. Dorothy and the couple’s three children returned to Ontario, and the photographed account records her death on November 6, 2010. Remembered within this church history, the family’s service and the response to violence continue the theme of Christian witness expressed through teaching, love, and the refusal to answer injury with hatred.

title: Daniel Gerber and Ruth Wilting

date.label: Vietnam service and loss, 1962–1968
date.basis: The panel dates Gerber’s abduction May 31, 1962; a contemporary obituary gives May 30. The narrative uses May 1962 and does not assign him a confirmed death date.

summary: Daniel Gerber’s alternative service and Ruth Wilting’s hospital work brought them to Vietnam, where Gerber disappeared after capture and Wilting was later killed.
paragraphs: Daniel Gerber went to Vietnam through alternative service with Mennonite Central Committee. He worked at a leprosarium, a hospital serving people with leprosy, at Ban Me Thuot, operated by the Christian and Missionary Alliance. Ruth Wilting, his fiancée, also worked at the hospital. Their shared setting was a work of care in the midst of an increasingly destructive conflict.

In May 1962, Gerber was captured with two other workers and taken away. The photographed panel gives May 31, while a contemporary obituary preserved by the Mennonite Library and Archives gives May 30. Both accounts remember his disappearance and the long absence of confirmed news. The panel’s heading, “1940–?”, leaves his death date unresolved; this history does not replace that uncertainty with an invented date.

Wilting returned home for a time and then went back to the hospital in Vietnam. She was killed in an attack in 1968. The two lives intersect in this account through Christian medical service and the cost borne by those who continued it. Gerber’s MCC role is explicitly Mennonite; the sources place Wilting in the Christian and Missionary Alliance hospital work and do not establish that she herself belonged to a Mennonite church.

title: Amish family and community life
summary: The photographed account connects Amish homes, schools, work, marriage, and burial with a shared life shaped by Christian conviction and community tradition.
paragraphs: The local Amish community in the photographed history is presented through an agrarian way of life. Horse-drawn travel and farm work, distinctive dress, and private schooling express an interwoven pattern of scriptural interpretation, tradition, simplicity, modesty, and nonconformity. These descriptions concern the communities represented in the source, rather than establishing identical customs for every Amish settlement.

Children learn within this life through play and practical responsibility. The panel shows them caring for animals, helping with gardening, and sharing activities with one another. Its school account describes education through eighth grade for most of the young people it discusses. The connection between home, work, and school prepares children to take their places in family and community life.

Marriage and burial bring the same community together at major passages in life. The wedding scene centers on the bridal couple and notes the customary blue shade of the bride’s dress in the setting depicted. The funeral scene gathers family and church around an open grave. Read together, the scenes show a community accompanying its members through ordinary days, new households, and the loss of loved ones.

title: Barn raising and mutual aid
summary: A community rebuilding after fire or disaster makes visible the mutual care that the photographed history associates with Christian love.
paragraphs: The barn-raising scene concerns more than the construction of a farm building. When fire or another disaster deprives a family of a barn, neighbors assemble to replace what has been lost and help restore the household’s means of work. The photographed account describes assistance crossing the boundary between Amish people and the non-Amish neighbors it calls “English.”

The emphasis is on willingness to help in a time of need. Differences between groups do not disappear, but the immediate suffering of a household calls the wider community together. Shared labor becomes a visible expression of care, and rebuilding a structure is also a way of helping a family recover its footing.

This theme belongs alongside the mutual provision described in Acts and the later history of Anabaptist common life and relief. The practices are not identical: a barn raising is a particular local response, while Hutterite community of goods and Mennonite relief agencies have different forms. What connects these accounts within the church’s history is the conviction that love for one another should take material and practical shape.

title: Gathered for worship
summary: The worship scenes present Amish, Hutterite, and Mennonite communities gathering in different settings while sustaining a shared life of faith.
paragraphs: The photographed timeline places three forms of gathered worship beside one another. In the Amish scene, households meet every other week in homes or associated buildings. The account describes German-language worship and men and women seated separately, facing one another. The gathering belongs to the rhythm of a local church district rather than to a permanently dedicated church building.

The Hutterite scene shows a meetinghouse, with men and women seated separately and facing forward. The Mennonite scene shows a church house with seating by family groups, while the caption acknowledges that some Mennonite congregations maintain separate seating for men and women. The source therefore records both recognizable patterns and variation within them.

These customs are historical descriptions of the communities represented, not a complete rulebook for every Anabaptist church. Their importance lies in how faith is carried in a gathering of people: listening, prayer, and common worship take place through forms learned and sustained within the community. The scenes link the public history of movements and migrations with the recurring congregational life those histories were meant to preserve.

title: Christian love carried into service
summary: The final globe scene joins the future of the church with the call to make God’s love in Jesus Christ known through both the gospel and practical service.
paragraphs: The closing globe scene places children before a vision of the worldwide church. Its explanation looks toward the church of tomorrow and states a purpose: that people throughout the world might know God’s love through Jesus Christ. The emphasis moves from the places where earlier communities lived to the continuing responsibility of those who receive their faith.

The panel connects this message with action. Love is to be expressed through service, a theme already embodied in the neighboring accounts of refugee accompaniment, education, hospital work, and help after disaster. The histories of the Dycks, the Groves, Daniel Gerber, and Ruth Wilting give particular names and settings to that larger calling.

The same panel prints a worldwide statistical snapshot attributed to Mennonite World Conference and marked “10/12.” It is a dated exhibit figure, not a present-day census. The church’s continuing history cannot be reduced to that count: the scene’s central claim is the Christian calling to pass on the faith and put love into practice across the world.

title: Mennonite migration to Germantown

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The 1683 Germantown settlement opened an important North American chapter in Mennonite migration.
paragraphs: The Concord reached Philadelphia on 6 October 1683 after a ten-week Atlantic voyage. On board were thirteen Mennonite-Quaker families from Krefeld. They settled in the Germantown area, beginning an important chapter of congregational and family life in Pennsylvania. The exhibit places their journey after the invitations associated with William Penn and George Fox.

The movement was followed by the work of establishing homes, trades, ministry, and places of worship. William Rittenhouse’s papermaking and pastoral work and the first log meetinghouse in 1708 show what settlement involved beyond the arrival of a ship. Later Swiss and German migration enlarged this North American history.

title: Settlement at Chortitza

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Communities established in the Russian Empire developed several church traditions and later migrated to the Americas and elsewhere.
paragraphs: The Chortitza settlement followed an extended process of invitation, investigation, and travel. The exhibit records that Prussian Mennonites sent Jacob Hoeppner and Johann Bartsch to examine land in 1786. An initial party left in 1788 and joined a larger company of families; after wintering in camp they resumed the journey in early 1789.

By 1800 the panel places about four hundred families in fifteen villages at Chortitza. Letters preserved by Mennonite Heritage Archives connect the settlers with the Prussian congregations they had left, including correspondence dated 1789. Their new home became a starting point for later colony histories and migrations, while the establishment of Molotschna in the next generation added another important center.

title: Kleine Gemeinde begins

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: A reform movement in the Molotschna settlement that began in 1812 under Klaas Reimer and later developed different national histories.
paragraphs: Klaas Reimer and other Mennonites at Molotschna organized the Kleine Gemeinde, or Little Church, in 1812. Their call for reform concerned church discipline and the conduct of Christian life. A separate fellowship allowed them to order congregational life according to those convictions within the wider settlement history.

Families migrated to Canada in 1874–1875, carrying this church identity with them. Later developments included the Canadian Evangelical Mennonite Conference, while other communities retained the Kleine Gemeinde name, including congregations in Mexico. The founding event is therefore the beginning of several later local histories, each of which needs to be followed through its own migrations and decisions.
