title: John Holdeman’s separate fellowship

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: John Holdeman and others began worshiping separately in Ohio in 1859, forming a distinct Mennonite church history.
paragraphs: In 1859 John Holdeman and a small group began worshiping separately in Wayne County, Ohio. Holdeman’s religious awakening and concern for the spiritual life of the church had led him to seek a preaching ministry that the existing congregation did not affirm. The new fellowship became the Church of God in Christ, Mennonite.

Holdeman traveled and wrote in support of renewal, including the work known as Mirror of Truth. Migration took followers to Missouri and Kansas, and converts from the Kleine Gemeinde in Manitoba joined the movement. The church’s account connects its beginning with conversion, believers’ baptism, nonresistance, and a disciplined common life.

title: The Mennonite Brethren emerge

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Renewal within Mennonite communities in the Russian Empire contributed to the formation of the Mennonite Brethren in 1860.
paragraphs: Bible-study groups and a call to renewed Christian life preceded the formation of the Mennonite Brethren in the Molotschna settlement in 1860. The movement developed within the church communities of the Russian Empire and gave institutional expression to concerns about conversion, discipleship, and congregational renewal.

The branch chart follows the new fellowship through migration and mission beyond the colony settlements. Abraham and Miriam Friesen’s departure for India in 1890 supplies one named example of that wider work. The Mennonite Brethren line has its own history alongside Kleine Gemeinde and other colony churches; its later growth can be followed through congregations, missions, and schools rather than through the founding date alone.

title: Hutterite migration to North America

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Hutterite communities began migrating from the Russian Empire to North America in the 1870s after changes affecting military exemption and community life.
paragraphs: Hutterite communities joined the wider movement from the Russian Empire to North America beginning in 1874. The exhibit links the decision to changing military-service requirements and concerns about preserving religious and communal life. For communities committed to nonresistance, the terms under which families would live and their young men would serve were matters of conscience.

The journey transferred more than people and farming skills. Hutterites sought to continue shared possessions and an ordered communal life in their new settlements. Their North American history did not end the testing of those convictions: wartime coercion in 1918, the ordeal of the Hofer brothers and Jacob Wipf, and the movement of colonies to Canada became later chapters of the same commitment.

title: Old Order Mennonite regional divisions

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Old Order Mennonite fellowships developed through several regional divisions beginning in the later nineteenth century.
paragraphs: In 1872 Jacob Wisler and supporters formed separate Mennonite conferences in Indiana and Ohio after disagreements over innovations in church life. Related regional separations followed in Ontario in 1889, Pennsylvania in 1893, and Virginia in 1901. These dates describe a sequence of decisions among different communities, not one universal founding meeting.

The Old Order line on the exhibit names several later fellowships, including Wisler, Martinite, Wenger, Woolwich, and Horning communities. They share concerns about ordered congregational life and continuity of practice, while particular rules and relationships differ. Each named fellowship needs its own local records; the regional chronology provides a starting framework without assigning every group an identical story.

title: The beginnings of the Bruderhof

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Eberhard and Emmy Arnold, together with Else von Hollander, founded the Bruderhof in Germany in 1920.
paragraphs: Eberhard and Emmy Arnold, together with Else von Hollander, began the Bruderhof at Sannerz in Germany in 1920. They sought a common life shaped by the Sermon on the Mount and the sharing described in Acts. The establishment of a household community gave practical form to their desire for renewed New Testament discipleship.

The later history included fellowship with Hutterites and movement across national borders. The supplied panel records acceptance into the Hutterian brotherhood in 1931 and the spread of Bruderhof communities to England, Paraguay, the United States, and Australia. Its own beginnings remain attached to the people and commitments of 1920, while subsequent relationships and relocations form further stages of the story.

title: A worldwide gathering

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The first Mennonite World Conference gathering was held in Basel in 1925. Later assemblies form part of the story of worldwide Anabaptist fellowship.
paragraphs: The first Mennonite World Conference assembly met at Basel, Switzerland, from 13 to 16 June 1925 under the presidency of Christian Neff. It commemorated the beginning of Anabaptism four centuries earlier and created an occasion for believers from different national settings to meet around a shared history.

The next gathering, at Danzig in 1930, addressed Mennonite relief and communities in the Soviet Union. Subsequent assemblies continued the fellowship across borders: the supplied chart follows meetings in Europe and North America and reaches Curitiba in Brazil in 1972 and Winnipeg in 1990. These gatherings made room for worship, testimony, and shared concerns without replacing the different participating churches with a single denomination.

title: Mennonite relief cooperation: MCC

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Mennonite Central Committee began in 1920 as a cooperative response to hunger among communities in Ukraine.
paragraphs: Hunger in Ukraine brought leaders from different North American Mennonite churches together at Elkhart, Indiana, on 27 July 1920. Thirteen leaders discussed how the churches could respond. The first official meeting of Mennonite Central Committee followed on 27 September. Its name expressed the decision to coordinate aid through one central body.

The exhibit places this organization in the aftermath of revolution, violence, and famine. Congregations sent help, and workers carried relief toward the affected communities. Clayton Kratz was among those who went and did not return. The story of MCC’s beginning therefore includes both cooperation across church lines and the personal cost of serving people in danger.

title: The Beachy Amish division

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Beachy Amish history began with a 1927 division in an Amish congregation in Somerset County, Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: The Amish congregation associated with Moses M. Beachy in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, divided in 1927. The dispute involved church discipline, including the treatment of members who transferred to other Anabaptist congregations. Questions about the ban and fellowship made the separation a matter of church order as well as local relationships.

The Beachy name later came to describe a wider Amish Mennonite fellowship. The source chart places this line within Amish history, alongside other communities that responded differently to changes in church practice. Later worship, transportation, and mission patterns should be traced through their own local records rather than all being assigned to the first dispute in 1927.

title: Rudnerweider church organization

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: A renewal movement among Sommerfeld Mennonites organized as the Rudnerweider church in 1937.
paragraphs: A renewal movement among Sommerfeld Mennonites led to the organization of the Rudnerweider church. The supplied chart marks the movement in 1936, while the official archival description dates church organization to 1937. These dates are retained as different stages rather than silently forcing the two sources into one year.

The new fellowship developed within the colony-based Mennonite history in Manitoba. It later adopted the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference name in 1959. Its archived congregational records, conference material, and mission history provide the evidence for following that development from a call for renewal into a continuing church organization.

title: Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Rudnerweider church adopted the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference identity on 1 July 1959.
paragraphs: The fellowship that had organized as the Rudnerweider church in 1937 adopted the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference identity on 1 July 1959. The archival description distinguishes the earlier organization from this later change of name, connecting both within one continuing history.

The chart places the conference among the colony-based Mennonite streams and follows its development from the Sommerfeld and Rudnerweider setting. Its archives preserve evidence of conference life, congregational activity, and mission. The similar Evangelical Mennonite Conference name belongs to the Kleine Gemeinde history, so the two lines retain separate records and relationships.

title: Evangelical Mennonite Conference name

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Canadian Kleine Gemeinde adopted the name Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960.
paragraphs: The Canadian Kleine Gemeinde took the name Evangelical Mennonite Church in 1952 and Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960. The change belongs to a history reaching back to Klaas Reimer’s renewal movement in Molotschna in 1812 and the migration of families to Manitoba in 1874–1875.

The new conference name became part of the organization’s continuing congregational and mission life. It did not rename every community descended from Kleine Gemeinde, some of which retained the older designation. The timeline therefore connects the Canadian conference to its earlier roots while preserving the distinct identities of related churches in other countries.

title: The Missionary Church union

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The exhibit’s Mennonite Brethren in Christ line developed into United Missionary Church and joined a union in 1969.
paragraphs: In 1969 the United Missionary Church and the Missionary Church Association united to form the Missionary Church. The supplied timeline traces the United Missionary line back through the Mennonite Brethren in Christ name and nineteenth-century evangelical and holiness renewal.

The union brought together two organizations with their own earlier histories. Reading the old names on the chart makes it possible to follow the sequence instead of treating every Brethren or Missionary label as the same church. title: Charity Christian Fellowship begins

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Charity Christian Fellowship began in Lancaster County in 1982 and developed a sermon ministry reaching wider fellowships.
paragraphs: Charity Christian Fellowship began in Lancaster County in 1982 through the work of Mose Stoltzfus and Denny Kenaston. Its own history describes a desire for revived New Testament church life. The congregation’s preaching and mission activity became the starting point for a wider sermon ministry.

Sermons circulated first through cassette distribution. The ministry adopted the Charity Gospel Tape Ministry name in 1990 and later became Charity Ministries. A joint ministry with Ephrata Christian Fellowship began in 2001. These developments distinguish the founding congregation from the wider distribution work and provide dated steps for following the fellowship’s influence beyond its local meetings.

title: Mennonite Church USA forms

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Mennonite Church USA formed in 2002 through the union of U.S. congregations of MC and GC.
paragraphs: Mennonite Church USA formed in 2002 when U.S. congregations from the Mennonite Church and General Conference Mennonite Church entered a new denominational organization. The two names appear separately on the supplied branch chart because each had a substantial history before the union.

The union supplies a later chapter for those particular U.S. church streams. Their archives preserve the earlier conferences, congregations, schools, missions, and shared institutions through which that history can be followed. Other Anabaptist fellowships and national church histories continued along their own paths, and the broader timeline keeps those continuing lines visible beside the new organization.

title: The Schwarzenau Brethren

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: A group baptized in the Eder River at Schwarzenau began a movement shaped by both Anabaptist convictions and Pietism.
paragraphs: In August 1708, five men and three women met at the Eder River in Schwarzenau for baptism on a personal confession of faith. An unnamed member baptized Alexander Mack, who then baptized the other seven. All had previously been baptized as infants, so the action placed them outside the religious order enforced by the authorities.

Their gathering expressed a commitment to live together under the guidance of the New Testament. The Church of the Brethren’s history connects the movement with peaceful action, plain and compassionate living, and active witness. Evangelists traveled to other communities; migration to Pennsylvania began in 1719, followed by the organization of a congregation at Germantown in 1723.

title: Anabaptist history is still being written

date.label: The living Anabaptist family
date.basis: Present-day context of this archive.

summary: The present-day story includes communities across continents and many different traditions. Local histories, migrations, mission, and relationships between churches are part of the record still being gathered.
paragraphs: The later pages of the supplied exhibit carry this history beyond Europe and North America to congregations and mission in Java, India, Congo, Argentina, and other countries. Refugees, missionaries, families, teachers, and relief workers all appear in that continuing story. Their experiences connect the older witness of faith and nonresistance with new places and responsibilities.

The living history includes worship, mutual aid, the teaching of children, care for people in danger, and the formation of new congregations and fellowships. Named branches have distinct local records and relationships that can be explored through their pages. title: Jorists: David Joris and the meaning of discipleship

date.label: 1536–1556 (David Joris’s later ministry)
date.basis: The 1536 Bocholt meeting and Joris’s death in 1556 frame this account. These are not founding and extinction dates for all Jorist communities.

summary: The Jorists appear in the Dutch portion of the chart as a distinct movement whose teachings nonresistant witnesses examined against Scripture.
paragraphs: The supplied chart places the Jorists beside other Dutch movements of the 1530s. Named for David Joris, this stream belonged to the unsettled years after Münster’s fall in 1535. GAMEO’s revised biography describes his efforts at Bocholt in 1536 to reconcile militant and peaceable factions, followed by increasing reliance on prophetic authority and spiritual interpretations of Christian practices.

Martyrs’ Mirror preserves a specific disagreement in Jacques D’Auchy’s examination, preceding his execution in 1559. D’Auchy rejects an interpretation attributed to Joris that replaces the actual breaking of bread with a spiritual meaning. Appealing to Acts 2:46 and Acts 20:7, he insists that the gathered believers really ate bread. This testimony concerns a particular doctrinal dispute, rather than documenting every follower’s life or convictions.

Joris moved to Basel in 1544 and died in 1556. His place in the chart helps explain distinctions early believers had to make; the proximity of chart lines does not establish that later nonresistant Mennonite branches descended from the Jorists.

title: Batenburgers: violence and the nonresistant witness

date.label: 1535–1544 (principal activity described here)
date.basis: The account follows the aftermath of Münster in 1535 through the execution of a later leader in 1544. GAMEO records later references; 1544 is not an extinction date.

summary: The Batenburgers’ separate line in the chart supplies context for the accusations of religious violence that peaceful Anabaptists had to answer.
paragraphs: The Batenburgers followed Jan van Batenburg, whose movement gathered adherents after Münster’s fall in 1535. GAMEO’s historical entry describes a group that permitted attacks and church plundering in expectation of divine judgment. Batenburg was captured in 1537 and executed in 1538; some adherents remained active after his death, and a later leader, Appelman, was executed in 1544.

The supplied Martyrs’ Mirror does not provide a Batenburg biography. It does preserve Jacob de Keersgieter’s 1569 answer to accusations about Münster and religious violence: he denies that such people were his brethren and rejects the attempt to establish Christ’s kingdom by force. The passage records the burden those accusations placed upon nonresistant believers; it does not identify every group involved by name.

The chart’s separate Batenburgers line therefore belongs to the surrounding history of competing claims and persecution. It should not become an inferred line of descent into the later Mennonite fellowships that confessed a peaceable following of Christ.

title: St. Gallen: Scripture, baptism, and a gathered community

date.label: 1525–1527 (early community)
date.basis: The major early movement and its suppression are dated 1525–1527 by GAMEO. The narrative separately identifies a regional testimony from 1529; the interval does not imply that all Anabaptist activity ended in 1527.

summary: St. Gallen became an early centre of believers’ baptism as public Scripture readings led townspeople to examine faith and the shape of the church.
paragraphs: At St. Gallen, east of Zürich, lay Scripture readings helped prepare the way for believers’ baptism. Lorenz Hochrütiner and Wolfgang Uliman were among those who questioned infant baptism and gathered listeners around the biblical message. On Palm Sunday, 9 April 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized many townspeople in the Sitter River. Sattler College’s account, drawing on contemporary chronicles, cautions that the precise number is unknown.

The new community soon faced restrictions on baptism and unauthorized meetings. GAMEO’s account describes fines and banishment in 1525 and a greatly weakened movement by the end of 1526. These pressures give the chart’s short St. Gallen line historical substance without proving that every local believer disappeared or that the line represents a later denomination.

The supplied Martyrs’ Mirror also preserves a regional connection: in a 1529 examination, Agatha Kampner said that she had been baptized near St. Gall. She defended preaching the Gospel and gathering to hear it, and declared her intention to remain faithful. Her testimony supplies a personal witness alongside the wider community history.
